query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiprincipal-element alloys (such as CrMnFeCoNi) for high‐temperature applications, the relative concentration of high‐affinity oxidation elements governs oxidation resistance and material integrity by controlling the nature of the surface oxide scale. Reducing Mn relative to Cr and/or Al will promote the formation of a dense, adherent, protective oxide layer (e.g., Cr2O3 and/or Al2O3) rather than non‐protective Mn-rich oxides, thus limiting Mn depletion and preserving mechanical integrity during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic or near-equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy in its as-cast or homogenized microstructure.
generation.intervention: Systematically adjust the alloy composition to reduce the relative Mn content while increasing Cr and/or Al content.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation in air at temperatures between 800°C and 1200°C over extended exposure times (e.g., 24–120 hours), with possible thermal cycling to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The nature and structure of the developing oxide scale – a dual-layer scale with an inner, adherent protective Cr2O3/Al2O3 (or mixed) layer and an outer sacrificial layer versus a non-protective, Mn-rich oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: Lowering Mn decreases its preferential outward diffusion and oxidation, thereby suppressing the formation of non-protective Mn-oxides (e.g., Mn3O4) that deplete the bulk alloy. In contrast, enriched Cr/Al promotes the early formation of a compact and stable oxide (Cr2O3/Al2O3) that acts as a diffusion barrier against oxygen and limits further elemental depletion, preserving mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy (with reduced Mn and increased Cr/Al) will exhibit a slower oxidation rate (lower oxide thickness and parabolic oxidation constant), improved oxide scale adhesion and integrity, and better retention of mechanical properties (e.g., minimal loss of strength due to reduced Mn depletion).
generation.baseline: The unmodified equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi alloy that forms predominantly non-protective Mn-rich oxides under high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for high-temperature oxidation in air within the 800°C to 1200°C range over exposure times from 24 to 120 hours. Outside of these conditions (e.g., different atmospheres or extreme thermal cycling beyond the tested regime), the governing mechanisms may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in oxidation kinetics and mechanical integrity may depend on additional microstructural factors (e.g., grain size, segregation) and the influence of minor alloying elements. Further investigation is needed to establish the exact compositional thresholds for optimal protective oxide formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one set with the baseline equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi composition and another set with a modified composition having reduced Mn and increased Cr and/or Al. Process both sets under identical conditions to ensure similar microstructures. Expose the specimens to controlled oxidation tests in air at temperatures between 800°C and 1200°C for durations of 24, 72, and 120 hours (with additional thermal cycling if desired). After exposure, characterize the oxide layers using in situ or ex situ XRD, SEM/EDS, and measure mass changes via thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). Mechanical integrity tests (e.g., hardness, tensile strength, or adhesion via critical load measurements) should also be conducted.
measurements: Oxide scale composition and thickness (via XRD and SEM/EDS)
Parabolic oxidation rate constant (via TGA/mass gain data)
Mechanical property retention (hardness, tensile strength, adhesion tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the modified alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements over the baseline in terms of reduced oxidation rate (i.e., similar oxide thickness/parabolic rate constant), formation of a clearly protective oxide scale (as evidenced by comparable scale chemistries and adhesion), and preservation of mechanical properties. In other words, if lowering Mn and increasing Cr/Al does not produce a more protective oxide scale and improve material integrity relative to the unmodified alloy under the specified conditions, the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, or Fe3O4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. While the Base Alloy exhibited a mass gain of approximately 15 mg/cm2 after oxidation at 900 °C for 120 h, the addition of Cr2.5Co2.5Mn2.5 promoted the formation of a multilayered oxide scale (outer MnCr2O4/inner Al2O3), reducing the parabolic oxidation rate constant to 1.7 × 10−5 mg2·cm−4·s−1. Unlike conventional oxidation-resistant alloy design strategies that mainly rely on complex alloying, this work demonstrates that the rapid solidification effect of laser cladding can generate nanocrystalline grain boundaries, which serve as fast diffusion channels for Al and Cr and promote the rapid formation of a protective MnCr2O4/Al2O3 bilayer scale. chosen.lever: alloy composition (specifically varying the content of elements that promote the formation of protective oxide scales)
chosen.technique: systematic high-temperature oxidation testing combined with advanced surface and cross-sectional characterization (SEM/EDX, XPS, and possibly TEM)
chosen.conditions: a controlled oxidizing environment over a temperature range of 800 °C to 1200 °C, where comparisons are made relative to a baseline multiprincipal-element alloy
chosen.why: This experiment directly fills the niche by testing a mechanistic hypothesis: that the oxidation resistance and overall material integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys are governed by the ability to form a stable, adherent protective oxide scale, which is controlled by the alloy’s composition. By systematically varying the content of key elements and comparing the oxidation kinetics and oxide microstructure under identical high-temperature conditions, the study provides clear, observable differences relative to a known baseline. Any deviation (e.g., no improvement or unexpected degradation) would falsify the hypothesis, while supporting evidence in the form of scale morphology and compositional gradients would reinforce it.

frame.system: Multiprincipal‐element alloys (high‐entropy alloys) in their as-cast or homogenized microstructure designed for high-temperature oxidation environments.
frame.goal: To elucidate the mechanistic determinants of oxidation resistance and mechanical integrity during prolonged high-temperature exposure by identifying which compositional and microstructural factors (e.g., selective elemental segregation and protective oxide scale formation) govern oxidation behavior.
frame.limitation: There is an open question about which intrinsic alloy features (such as elemental affinities, diffusion rates, and scale formation tendencies) control the development of protective versus non-protective oxide scales in harsh, sustained high-temperature conditions.
root_cause_cues: sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments
constraints: The hypothesis must be testable via controlled comparisons against a baseline composition or treatment.
Observations should predict distinct differences (e.g., scale composition, adhesion, and growth kinetics) relative to a baseline alloy.
The experimental design must span a defined range of temperatures and exposure durations to ensure the hypothesis holds over the intended operating conditions.
A clear falsification criterion is required.
frame.regime: High-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 800–1200°C) with prolonged exposure and possibly thermal cycling to mimic service conditions.

decision.trend: Research on oxidation mechanisms in multiprincipal‐element alloys has advanced from empirical measurements of overall scale thickness and degradation rates to in‐situ characterization that deconvolutes which elements oxidize preferentially. Early studies identified the problem of non-protective oxide formation without a clear causal link, while later studies using in‐situ XRD and atom probe tomography (PMC10384371 and PMC11169556) demonstrated that selective oxidation (e.g., Mn or Cr contributions) and element redistribution can dictate oxide structure. Most recently, work integrating compositional modifications (e.g., Cr, Co, Mn and trace Y additions as in PMC13208696) has shown that tailored alloy composition can drive the formation of a dual‐layer oxide scale (protective inner and sacrificial outer) with markedly improved oxidation kinetics. This progression—from empirical observation to advanced, targeted composition tuning—has set the stage for directly testing mechanistic hypotheses under controlled comparisons.
decision.unsolved: Despite these advances, a clear, testable mechanistic hypothesis that quantitatively links specific compositional adjustments (and the resulting segregation/diffusion kinetics) to the formation of protective versus non‐protective oxide scales over a defined temperature and exposure range remains to be established. In other words, the relative roles of elemental affinities (e.g., competition between Mn and Cr/Al) in governing oxidation resistance and subsequent material integrity have not been pinned down via a controlled baseline comparison.
decision.lever: systematic tuning of high‐affinity oxidation element concentrations (e.g., adjusting Mn versus Cr/Al ratios)
decision.why: Building on recent trends that reveal selective elemental segregation as key to protective scale formation, the most plausible next step is to design a controlled experiment where a baseline alloy is directly compared against variants with tailored concentrations of elements known to form either protective or non‐protective oxides. Such an experiment—incorporating in‐situ high‐temperature oxidation tests (at, e.g., 800–1200°C) with mass change monitoring and post‐exposure electron microscopy—will isolate the influence of these compositional levers on oxide chemistry and adhesion, precisely addressing the open question regarding which intrinsic features govern oxidation resistance and material integrity.
